objective: Students will identify the major cell organelles (nucleus, mitochondria, ribosome, cell membrane, chloroplast) and explain each one's function, then use structure-function reasoning to predict which organelles a specialized cell needs and to distinguish plant from animal cells.
hook: Every one of your trillions of cells is a microscopic factory running 24/7 — and today you'll meet the workers on the floor.
agenda: Bell ringer (5) · Mini-lesson: the cell as a factory (12) · Label & match (8) · Practice (17) · Exit (3)
assessment: The exit ticket checks whether each student can name at least one organelle and state its correct function in their own words — the core objective for the day.

script.title: Bell ringer
script.do: Project a labeled factory image beside a labeled animal-cell diagram. Have students silently jot one guess: 'If a cell is a factory, what part is the boss?' Take 2-3 quick answers.
options: Ask students to list every cell part they already remember from middle school on a sticky note
script.say: Every part of a factory has a job — by the end of today you'll match each cell part to its job the same way.

script.title: Mini-lesson: the cell as a factory
script.do: Walk the launch slides. For each organelle, give the factory analogy, then the real function, and have students fill the notes: nucleus = control room/DNA, mitochondria = power plant/ATP, ribosome = assembly line/protein synthesis, cell membrane = security gate, chloroplast = solar panel (plants only). Then contrast plant vs. animal cells.
options: Use a physical model or a build-a-cell drawing on the board if no projector
script.say: The mitochondria are the power plant — they release the energy, as ATP, that runs everything else.

script.title: Label & match
script.do: Students complete Section 1 (match organelle to job) with an elbow partner while you circulate and check for the classic mix-up between ribosome and nucleus. Review answers aloud.
options: Do it as a whole-class card sort with organelle cards taped to the board
script.say: Read the job first, then ask yourself: which worker in the factory does exactly that?

script.title: Practice
script.do: Students work Sections 2 and 3 independently, then compare short answers with a partner. Circulate and push students to justify the muscle-cell mitochondria answer with the idea that muscle cells do a lot of work and therefore need a lot of energy/ATP.
options: Turn Section 2 into a stand-up 'four corners' where each corner is a letter choice
script.say: For the muscle-cell question, connect the dots: more work means more energy, and energy comes from…?

script.title: Exit
script.do: Hand out the exit ticket. Students name one organelle and its job in their own words and turn it in at the door.
options: Collect as a verbal ticket-out-the-door, one organelle per student, no repeats
script.say: One organelle, one job, your own words — that's your ticket out.

presentation.title: Cell Structure: The Cell as a Factory

slides.heading: A cell is a tiny factory
bullets: The cell = a factory, and each organelle is a worker with one main job
No single part does everything — the jobs are divided up
Today: meet the main organelles and what each one does

slides.heading: Organelles & jobs
bullets: Nucleus — the control room; holds DNA and directs the cell
Mitochondria — the power plant; releases energy as ATP
Ribosomes — the assembly line; make proteins
Cell membrane — the security gate; controls what enters and exits
Chloroplast (plants only) — the solar panel; carries out photosynthesis

slides.heading: Plant vs. animal cells
bullets: Both have: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, cell membrane, cytoplasm
Plant cells ALSO have: a rigid cell wall (support), chloroplasts (photosynthesis), and one large central vacuole (stores water)
Animal cells have small vacuoles, no cell wall, and no chloroplasts
Reason: plants make their own food from sunlight; animals eat food instead

slides.heading: You try
bullets: A hardworking muscle cell contracts constantly and burns a lot of energy
Which organelle would it have a LOT of, and why?
Answer with the structure-function link: heavy work → high energy demand → many mitochondria (more ATP)

vocab.definition: The control center of the cell; it stores the cell's DNA and directs the cell's activities.
The organelle that releases energy for the cell by breaking down food to make ATP; often called the powerhouse of the cell.
The tiny organelle that builds proteins by linking amino acids together (protein synthesis).
The thin outer boundary that surrounds the cell and controls what materials enter and leave it.
An organelle found only in plant cells (and some protists) that captures sunlight to make food through photosynthesis.

notes:
## Cell Structure
**Big idea:** a cell is like a factory — each organelle has a specific job, and no single part does everything.

**Organelles → jobs:**
- **Nucleus** → the control room; stores DNA and directs the cell.
- **Mitochondria** → the power plant; release energy as ATP.
- **Ribosomes** → the assembly line; make proteins.
- **Cell membrane** → the security gate; controls what enters and leaves the cell.
- **Chloroplast** → the solar panel; does photosynthesis (PLANT cells only).

**Plant vs animal:**
- Both have a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, cell membrane, and cytoplasm.
- Plant cells ALSO have a **cell wall** (support/shape), **chloroplasts** (photosynthesis), and a **large central vacuole** (stores water).
- Animal cells have no cell wall, no chloroplasts, and only small vacuoles.

**Structure to function:** a cell's job predicts its organelles. Cells that work hard (like muscle cells) need lots of energy, so they carry many mitochondria to make more ATP.

sections.type: Match the organelle to its job
sections.directions: Write the organelle next to its function.
problems: Controls the cell and stores DNA → ?
Controls what enters and leaves the cell → ?
A cell that uses a LOT of energy would have many: (A) ribosomes (B) mitochondria (C) vacuoles (D) cell walls
Which is found in PLANT cells but NOT animal cells? (A) nucleus (B) mitochondria (C) chloroplast (D) ribosome
Explain the 'cell as a factory' analogy using two organelles and the job each one does.
🌶 A muscle cell and a skin cell are both human cells, but the muscle cell has far more mitochondria. Explain why using the idea of energy.
Name one structure found in plant cells but not animal cells, and describe its job.

answerKey.section: Match the organelle to its job

answers: (B) mitochondria — they make ATP, so an energy-hungry cell needs many of them
(C) chloroplast — it does photosynthesis and is found only in plant cells

Sample: A cell is like a factory where each organelle has a job. The nucleus is the control room that stores the DNA and directs the cell, and the ribosomes are the assembly line that makes the proteins. (Any two correctly matched organelles and jobs earn credit.)

Sample: Muscle cells contract and do a lot of work, so they need a lot of energy. Mitochondria release energy as ATP, so a cell that uses more energy needs more mitochondria to supply it. Skin cells work less, so they need fewer.
Sample: Chloroplast — it captures sunlight and carries out photosynthesis to make food. (Cell wall — provides support and shape; or large central vacuole — stores water — are also acceptable.)

exitTicket: Name one organelle and its job in your own words.
